game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
All of my yes.

It is definately a narrative driven, "expirience" with some choices and consequences in between, you uncover a terrorist plot while actively invading the privacy of anyone who is involved.

Gameplay consists of datamining private and public information and deciding which snipets of data you upload to Orwell (meaning the governemtn agencies have now access to it and act accordingly) as well as trying to deduce and pick out the right choice between conflicting pieces of data (there isn't always a "best" answer) as you race to uncover and stop a domestic terrorist group. Most of these happen without the pressure of time on you, but in cruicial moments events become time sensitive, with what informaton you upload and how fast you do it affects events on the fly as they unfold.

Orwell explores the idea of universal electronic surveilance (with some safeguards, the former of which is you, the player character who acts as a firewall between the government agency you work for and the private data of The Nations citizens) by putting it in an non-abstract, non-dystopian "present day" domestic terrorism scenario. There are multiple avenues that it refects on and the story told is enjoyable and avoids some of the tried cliches of genre fiction. 

Can't wait for the rest of the episodes. Wort the price of admission in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

The story telling was amazing, tho a bit too *I am waiting for an animation to skip* 
It was fun, but definitely deserves to be played with time and clear mind. 
Now if you will excuse me, I will try to disconnect from Orwell

The plot is very interesting, the writing is on the nose- reading people's texts etc seems exactly like it would in real life. I feel like they could of gone much deeper, and I hope they'll make another season. Easy point and click. Seems to save automatically at certain points but doesn't make you aware. I had a power outage while playing that eerily timed up with something similar in the game and freaked me right out. But It picked up right where it left off. Seems to have multiple outcomes, in order to get all the achievements- so good re-playability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Orwell [/h1] is a very interesting game to say the least. While gameplay wise you just have to pull and drag some text into a box, the story is captivating as well as how you influence it.

[b] Gameplay [/b]: So Orwell is a game where you embody Big Brother or more like a part of it, an essential yet very subjective part. You goal will be to choose and extract informations on people from their websites, social medias and other public informations but also the data inside their cellphone, personal computer, private phone calls and message, crossing the border of privacy. You interfere with the story by choosing what information are revelante or not, making you think about which information you want to upload or not to Orwell (the Big Brother server). Futhermore choosing to upload one information can make others being not uploadable because it has some conflict with it (2 piece of information can say opposite thing, it's up to you to choose which one is legit or not). this will makes you even more careful about it, and that's good because even if I just had to pull and drag some text, I really got tense during some phase of the game. Felt very immersive

[b] Art [/b] : The art for the pictures is a tad special, but I liked it a lot. The interface is well done and very comfortable to browse. 

[b] Musics and sounds [/b] : The music really got me in this game, I first expected not bad but plane music for this game but it's really not the case. I think that the music is a big factor of why I got this tense (in a good way) in that not so tense pull and drag gameplay. When something bad happens (or will happen) I felt like I had to do things faster even if this game never had timer or whatsoever like it and that you have all your time.

[b] Story [/b] : The characters that you will dig in their privacy are fairly good, they all have interesting personality and felt really human. Story wise it's a little predictable but, well you ARE the big brother so you had every pieces to know what will happen but what I want to focus on is how you influense the story. In the gameplay part I said that what you want to focus on is wheter a piece of information is revelant or not, but that's not quite true if you don't want to be controlled by big brother, you are a small part of it but an essential one, and indirectly you are the one who control the police and the media in this game, so instead of contribute to big brother you can do the opposite, to give you some ideas. (This game have multiple endings and variations depending of which pieces of information you upload or not)

[b] Summary [/b] :

Pros : 
- The story and mostly how you influence it
- The music
- Fairly good characters 

Cons :
- Maybe a tad short even with the multiple endings but it is a wonderful game so I can't really blame it

90/100 I really enjoyed this game, it's refreshing and really fun and captiving to play. Actually I played a game which is similar to this one before but with puzzle too, the name is Replica and if you played Orwell and liked it you should look into Replica which is a pretty good game (not as good as this one if I recall but well, maybe I am wrong because it has been some times since I last played it, I will look into again and make a review) Still Orwell is not something you should miss, while it is short, I have only found one game that is similar and they are both very good so it's refreshing. If you are bored of your usual AAA games then that's maybe what you need.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

review_text_raw:
Ok Honestly this game is a treat. Incredibly interesting themes showing a modern interpretation of the prologue to 1984 in a sense. The mechanics work really well, making your decisions hold weight and using your own progress play into the games narrative hands (you'll see what I mean near the end). The music is well done too, a lovely little score playing in the background that never became annoying and felt at ease with the visuals and what I was doing, with some incredibly well timed swells in music and emotion as twists were revealed, something rather hard for a game which is mostly reading.
To explain what made me love the game is to describe a singular moment. Orwell floods you with information that seems useful and useless at the same time, using a highlighting system where certain phrases, words, numbers are made available to you to drag over to the left and thus profile your target. This occurs while reading throught the information, so it will pop up and if you are lazy, make you reliant on it, you may rush through the first couple hours just relying on this system, easy enough. But there was a point where I had to choose between two pieces of information to submit, and none of the lists of highlights I had collected seemed to help. Thankfully I like to take my time with my games and so had been reading everything carefully for intentions of characters and the like. Which made it all the more satisfying and magical when it clicked. When I realised that I had vague recollections of a small part of a post that I had read 30 minutes ago (I did say I like to take my time). This post had no highlights. The mechanics had not made me look at it. There was no cue on screen saying, "looking at this bit may help you decide on your answer". It was just me and my memory, rewarding me for actually paying attention to the game, I felt intelligent and attentive, even more so when it helped me make the correct choice without relying on luck.
I'm even going to replay it, something I've never done with an intensely story driven game like this, where I know how it unfolds. This will easily stay in my top ten for a long time I think.
There are only a couple of niggles I have on this game, one is that I kind of wish we had multiple cases to go through  instead of the large overarching one to see different uses and consequences to the use of Orwell, and the other is a technical one. At some point the game froze oddly and I had to quit out of the application, but thankfully the autosave is pretty damn sold and I never lost more than a few seconds of gameplay, I assume every action is autosaved and is the reason fo that.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Point-and-drag game that managed to strike me into deepest psychological state of mind.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a game where you play as an investigator hired outside the Nation. Your task is to discover a crime detail by searching from suspects' background information which you can gather around the web, to be later uploaded into Orwell security program. You will be accompanied by a single adviser in your every work session, their task will revolve around information that you put into Orwell, for them to act based on your input.

The game sets you into the day at the time a bombing is occurred at a public place. Your first day would revolve around investigating who's behind this bombing. You could work all-day long if you want and maybe put all the datachunks - highlighted information - available into Orwell [spoiler]since you are not "timed" until Episode 5[/spoiler], easy as is. But of course, the common ground is to double-check whether a datachunk is valid to your investigation, or they were there only as mere decorations of information scattered freely on web. Your understanding of validity will be tested, well, more or less.

The music managed to keep me into focus, with not too over-exaggerated tunes (listened to them on Spotify and looped them for some time). There are some tense moments - indicated by shock-therapy tune - where you have to choose which info is MORE valid among the other. You will be the judge of things revolving around the web information, but you know what to do. You have been trusted by the Nation to work with them, but are they trusted enough? Theoretically, they should be, giving the ability to build this seemingly-flawless program where you could uncover the truth of these people you're given task to keep an eye on.

Finishing the game, I'm telling you, they indeed work like a charm. Too well.

Oh, also low poly art-style. New term and style to adore in general.

Nitpicks that I have after discussing this with a fellow online investigator:
- I don't have any complaint for the mechanics, but I was hoping we could select our own datachunks instead of being presented in-game. [i]Then again it would be possibly overkill.[/i]
- Having voice actors for the call sessions would be nice, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]but then it was covered in the sequel which I have yet to get into.[/i][/url] So giving that one a pass.
- Calls and ongoing chats cannot be skipped during episode replay. I don't see a button or tutorial to archive the calls for later... [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]in which they covered this in the sequel, too.[/i][/url] This kills the will to replay the game under the same save file due to inefficiency, [i]unless it's not meant to punish the replayability?[/i]
- I read this somewhere, but calls and chats would start to roll AFTER we clicked on their names. Even when you left the game for coffee or lunch, it won't play until you click on it - making them "the most tolerate group of terrorists one has to deal with". [spoiler]The only uncontrollable moment is on the last episode's final call.[/spoiler]
Keep in mind I didn't need these to be implemented in the game - as they're all already covered in the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/]sequel[/url]. It would be too much of a work for the developers, as the game is already a success in the first place without these, anyway. 

Overall, Orwell managed to capture the feel of spying people to get info under the surface of the known. Which makes this game as one of my favorites, enough to delve deeper into privacy breach.


Be wary, always be open for possibilities.

review_text_raw:
Will just jump right into it , given that companies like facebook are throwing our privacy to the wolves(hackers), 3rd party ads etc , this is a perfect time to try out something like orwell to see really how accessing things that are meant to be private can lead to consequences....

If you have played something like papers please then this should be very easy for you to pick up and play , just like it you are a invesitgator recuited to check on a terror attack that took place using the Orwell program. 

At first things seem to be good you are hailed for you work... but how far are you willing to go to nail people to get caught just by selecting their words and thoughts for the moment taken by invading their private life , there are consequences for almost every thing you do.....

I would recommend taking it easy and finishing the game in one go and experiencing the consequences of your actions, without looking up on anything , you can do more playthroughs or go back to chapters to select different paths.
It's an amazing game which will keep asking you the question how far will you let yourself pick on things people say in pirvate . will you do your job as a investigator or follow your ethics ?

Some pros and cons i would like to point out -

Pros 
- Solid game with a proper story and atmosphere to match it.
- Choices there is no game over you play the game and finish in the way you want.
- Covers a lot of real world apps that you can easily connect the dots too.
- Sweet twists in plot will have you clicking around furiously....hehe

Cons
- There is a insanely long load time once you start the game causing many people to think maybe the game is stuck. Also pain if you happened to close the game by mistake will have to sit through the loading again.
- sometimes the hitbox completely misses what you select , this could be a disaster if there is a timed event going on, also for some reason overlay might stop responding (chapter 5)
- Sometimes the indicator which shows whats new to check out might not update casuing you to think that you missed reading something, also sometimes that hints are pretty vaugue leading to some annoying going back to older articles to check if something was missed.
- The ending ....it barely points to anything that there will be a second part or some shocking end game story<after credits> hinting to a second game but if you check the steam store there is a follow up game to this :D .

Overall if you are in the dark as to way some people are extermely worried/against letting their privacy lost that easily check this game out , loved it easily a 8/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Having followed this game for a while, waiting for the episodes to release, and meeting the devs at PAX, I can say that this was probably one of the most unique "point and click" experiences I've ever had. I can't even go into much detail, because I truly want you to experience this game for yourself, but there are a few things I will say:

+The game really does a good job of making the in-game world feel "real". From a terse, yet thorough, well-thought explanation to "The Nation's" geopolitcal standing, to the online advertisements and clickbait filler that often pepper the relevant articles

+All of the characters have very distinct, memorable lives, and you'll have a chance to explore each and every one of them. There are no characters which get passed over, and this really drives home the point that what you're doing is very 1984. You're not just seeing information relevant to your case, you're seeing ALL of the information.

+The audio. There is, quite frankly, very little music or ambient noise in the game, but this is actually a positive point for this title. Whenever you come across a particularly shocking datachunk, this intense riff plays, and maintains itself until you move on. I often found myself hearing the music before I realized what I was actually looking at, and it made me super excited to keep reading.

-The episodes did feel rather short, despite there being a lot of content in each. This is offset by the fact that you're not paying per episode. When you buy the game, you get the whole game, not just episode one.

-There was a mechanic near the end (not a spoiler), where you are given a limit on how many data chunks you could upload, given the explanation that "as you know, datachunks cost time". This was never really well illustrated in earlier episodes, and, while you were scolded for uploading silly or irrelevant information (such as Cassandra's location being "over the rainbow and into wonderland" in the first episode), you were never really penalized at all unless you uploaded the incorrect answer for a conflicting (yellow) datachunk. I think the entire "limited datachunk" mechanic could have been implemented a bit better, since the player was previously unprepared to deal with that. I think that perhaps an actual time limit (via countdown timer) would have made the whole thing seem a bit more frenzied, instead of the player idly dawdling, and having time to carefully consider their decisions.


All in all, this was a great game, and I seriously look forward to seeing more great ideas come out of this developer!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1][url=store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/]Orwell[/url] presents a decent diminutive mystery with pertinent social commentary through a very unique, novel yet straightforward approach to interactive storytelling.[/h1]

The game first asks you to create an investigator profile through its polished interface, effectively recruiting you in the ranks of Orwell, followed by a stylish low-poly security footage opening that sets the stage for the ongoing investigation. Your role is essentially to play the human element in what would otherwise be an extremely complex data mining algorithm in a surveillance system.

Gameplay in many ways feels like browsing through restrained web pages obtained through a very limited portion of the internet. You select which datachunks to upload to Orwell's server, which in turn unlock more related headlines, websites, restricted documents, private emails, bank accounts, and eventually tap into phone and text conversations between suspects.

New bookmarks just appear by themselves as revealed by your adviser. You don't have any actual research to do, all important clues are automatically highlighted, and as such the game first appears to be completely linear and rather easy. There is initially no clear reason not to upload data other than rare instances with conflictual information, where only one of two bits can be sent.

Then it gets a bit more complex and the story evolves into a satisfyingly more sophisticated mystery with multiple threads to investigate. You can decide to withhold information that you judge inadequate or untrue, and your choices can have pretty severe consequences in some cases. While there are few or no time sensitive actions, tension builds up a lot in the final chapter where you have a limited number of uploads available before a major event triggers.

There is no undo and your decisions clearly define paths that lead to multiple endings. One-way conversations with your adviser also create a pretty unique relationship.

Be prepared for lots and lots of reading. The game features sparse audio and pleasant low-poly aesthetics, but too few rendered footage and no voice overs.

The game's world also feels relatively small scale with only about a dozen significant characters in the story, despite a background of terrorism and international tension. Another odd thing is when you gain access to a suspect's PC or smartphone, only a handful of files are shown. This limited scope nevertheless keeps things manageable.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What an incredible game. I sat down hoping to start and finish a game in one sitting, and I did just that, just over 6 and a half hours later.

The game has you scouring websites and messages to begin with, later involving phone calls and electronic devices too. This action tickles a very specific investigative soft spot, allowing you to accept or reject information as you see fit (with some plot-progression-required points aside). Unfortunately this comes with the caviat that your -intention- is not always understood when making these choices, but the game does the best it can to inform you how the data will be interprited, while staying in-universe.

Now I have to make this very clear: I thought this game was completely different, based on the trailer I watched. I thought I would be monitoring areas using CCTV and pulling up profiles on potential criminals with Watchdogs-style hackery. This couldn't be further from the truth - this is an interactive visual novel through-and-though, much like a previous game I've played, and would highly recommend, Analogue: A Hate Story.

While playing this game I felt genuine emotions, which does not happen often. I felt elation at preventing an attack--something I felt I had complete control over, not just interaction with--and guilt over a death--one I know I caused, but could have potentially stopped with information I realised I had overlooked too late. It's like a more relaxed version of Telltale's The Walking Dead games, where your choices have sincere impact on the world. But don't think it's all just casual browsing either, as there are timed occurances that you need to be quick on your mouse to prevent, should you choose to. Sometimes you have to make uninformed choices, which you will simply have to live with the consequences of, while giving you hindsight for future playthroughs.

All in all, it was a fascinating story and premise that kept my attention for its duration, with the clear possibility of replayability, should you want to see all possible outcomes (and right your wrongs). You couldn't ask for more than that.

This couldn't be further from the truth - this is an interactive visual novel through-and-though, much like a previous game I've played, and would highly recommend, Analogue: A Hate Story. While playing this game I felt genuine emotions, which does not happen often. I felt elation at preventing an attack--something I felt I had complete control over, not just interaction with--and guilt over a death--one I know I caused, but could have potentially stopped with information I realised I had overlooked too late. It's like a more relaxed version of Telltale's The Walking Dead games, where your choices have sincere impact on the world. But don't think it's all just casual browsing either, as there are timed occurances that you need to be quick on your mouse to prevent, should you choose to. Sometimes you have to make uninformed choices, which you will simply have to live with the consequences of, while giving you hindsight for future playthroughs. All in all, it was a fascinating story and premise that kept my attention for its duration, with the clear possibility of replayability, should you want to see all possible outcomes (and right your wrongs). You couldn't ask for more than that.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR
It is a refreshing experience where you can easily see the hard work and love that went into making it.

Review:

Orwell is a love letter to Orwellian fiction. It is a plot filled with mystery and intrigue that evolves fast enough so you will never think about getting bored. I especially enjoyed how the game doesn’t paint the organization you work for as inherently bad/evil. Flawed, but in a way that makes it real, not malicious. This gives each individual person the chance to come to their own conclusions about this potential future.

There are a few issues with this game such as certain data chunks having potentially vague outcomes (much like a Bioware dialog wheel). Also the slow writing in personal messages, while realistic, did get a bit tiresome where you can read the text 3 times faster than they can type. And sadly you cannot walk away, wait for the convo to finish, and then come back, as certain data chunks are time sensitive (I learned this lesson the hard way). All those issues are trivial however and I did not feel that they ever interfere with my ability to play and enjoy the game; a minor annoyance. The ending however, did rub me the wrong way. 

Without spoiling anything, I will just say that the ending is multiple choice depending on how you act. Initially I enjoyed this reveal, yet ended up accidentally choosing an ending I did not want, after not being bale to figure out how to select the one that would make the most sense with my character/play style. Then once I realized what I had done I tried to go back, however once you beat the game that save file is forever stuck at the epilogue after the choice. This requires you to complete an additional play through.

With all that said I would definitively recommend this game!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't normally write reviews, but I think I have to here. If you have any interest in narrative structure, or if you like detective novels, I strongly recommend this game.

The title may be somewhat misleading, as Orwell is not, in fact, set in a horrible dystopian nightmare future brought about by an overavundance of surveillance. In fact, The Nation seems like a pretty decent place to live.

You play an investigator operating the new "Orwell" surveillance system, the most advanced data trawler/compiler ever. It's your job to upload relevant information pertaining to a series of people who may be connected to a terrorist attack. Due to the Orwell Code of Ethics, only investigators are allowed to upload things to Orwell. As a result, based on what you upload, other characters will make some very important, potentially disastrous decisions.

The game plays at quite a sedate pace, allowing you plenty of time to mull over what would be the most accurate and relevant information to allow everyone to make the best decisions they can, which is nice. What's even better is that this really makes it incredibly tense when the game DOES put you on a (usually very short) timer and forces you to make a snap decision that could get people killed.

The narrative has pulled a few dick moves so far (mainly of the "Well that would have been good to know 30 seconds ago" variety), but none of them seem unfair, and they're entirely believable.

As a final big tick in my "things that make a good narrative game" box, the characters all act generally sensibly and behave as you would expect rational human beings in high stress situations to behave.

tl;dr - 10/10 would upload again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An interesting puzzle/story game with a heavy-handed message.

Gameplay revolves around using a web-browser-like interface to look for information on persons of interest.  The interface is completely adequate for that purpose and that's about all you can say about the mechanics of the game.  

I'm not sure that the game has a Lose-State so you're essentially free to do whatever you want which is cool.  Personally, I'd have liked a few more red herrings or maybe a thing where my handler buddy gets weirded out while I obsessively upload as many pictures of everyone that I could find.  Also, I enjoyed the time limit aspect of one part of the game and seeing that in other places would have been cool.

The story and writing do all the heavy lifting for the game and I feel like it did a good job.  The scenario is fairly realistic and the characters are written well enough that you can get a feel for what's going on without things feeling too obvious, contrived, or arbitrary... except for one thing: there is an ending that (as far as I can tell) is entirely missing from the game and it feels like a missed opportunity to not allow players to pursue it.  I'm sure it's entirely intentional but I disagree with it.

Anyhow, the game's got 5 episodes and each of those take about an hour to complete.  I'd say it's well worth it if you can pick it up for 10bux or less.

review_text_raw: I was only intending to come back to this shortly to 100% the game, but I was very quickly reminded how excellent of an experience Orwell Season 1 is. The game has choice-based gameplay ala Telltale and Quantic Dream but is much more nuanced in its approach, allowing mostly complete freedom over what information the player decides to upload and share to this program. The story is very interesting and has a few plot twists to keep things interesting, and these are perfectly timed as well, occurring almost exactly when you think you've figured it out. Despite the game being entirely text and image based, it succeeds in being significantly more interesting than some higher budget titles which put a lot more time into their narratives. The soundtrack is also surprisingly good, and is even dynamic to an extent, changing when you read certain bits of texts that have reveals in them. It's a great time, doesn't overstay its welcome and is the perfect price, so I'd highly recommend it. 9/10.

This game is beautifully self paced - you click on things as you feel like clicking on them - so it's a much more comfortable game to play. There are a few minor irritations. Occasionally you are forced to click things that are meaningless and other times you can't click things that should be meaningful, but nothing to major. The story is sinister and well crafted. All 'round, it's good dystopian fun!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Had it lying in my library and decided to give it a try - it's surprisingly good!

Don't let the looks of a "static reading game" fool you, it's interactive and exciting even if you read and drag-drop most of the time. You are tasked with investigating an incident. As you scan through each evidence, you are often required to make decisions by your judgement and reasoning. These decisions are rewarding and often times impactful to the story. Paired with well-timed music and sound effects, the game becomes exciting as you unfold each piece only to discover one hidden truth and the rabbit hole behind it. Best of all, it includes multiple thought-provoking ending with a surprising plot-twist!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I would reccomend this game, as the concept is really decent... but the execution is not quite up to standard.
If anything, this is a text-only version of 'Her Story' which is a far superior game. Go buy it now - seriously.

The problem is that this kind of game should provide you all the information at the start and give you a time limit to piece together the narrative - giving you the choice between stopping terrorists or finding more out about a potenally corrupt gov?

 Instead it forces you to follow a narrative story which feels quite detached from your choices apart from a select few.

review_text_raw: Nice game covering the possibilities and dangers of surveillance systems. Plays good homage to it's title reference. Has enough story depth, character development and detective work to keep you interested. Some gameplay elements don't feel very intuitive, i found myself just grabbing all grabbable data chunks more often then not and only realizing very near the end that what i picked actually mattered to the ending. Could have maybe benefited from an earlier introduction of the timer thing? Not sure. Artwork was good, music ok. Overall good value for it's price and you can easily also catch it on sale. Looking forward to playing season 2.

review_text_raw:
As far as interactive visual novels go, I think this is one of the best. I'm a little bit disappointed with the final act. Although it is quite suspenseful, it could have been a little bit longer or just have a time limit instead of the limit used for day 5. Planning to revisit it again someday or pick up the follow-up on a sale.
Recommended, although not a masterpiece.
Btw, if you're already here and did not read the 1984 or Animal Farm, do yourself a favor and give them a browse. You're welcome!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If you enjoy non-timer dependent games and detective aims, Orwell is a suitable game for you. I liked the free will and non-pressure atmosphere, and also the story is very catching. You are part of the government's control area, kind of a research department, and you have to investigate all about the suspects' lives. 

Moreover, if you are a George Orwell's (the writer) enthusiast, you will find lots of resemblances with the autor's work.
